story.headline: Lebanon abolishes death penalty
story.summary: Lebanon's parliament voted to abolish capital punishment, the first Arab and Middle Eastern state to do so, replacing death sentences with life imprisonment at hard labour.
story.display_body: Lebanon's parliament abolished the death penalty on Tuesday 11 August, making the country the first Arab state — and the first in the Middle East — to strike capital punishment from its books. A majority of the 128-seat assembly backed the bill after amendments, with the bloc of the Iran-aligned Shia movement Hezbollah the notable exception, according to the speaker's office. The law replaces death sentences with life imprisonment at hard labour; Lebanon had already observed an unofficial moratorium on executions since 2004, and the Justice Ministry's prisons directorate counted 85 people under death sentence at the end of 2025, whose sentences now fall to be commuted. Rights groups have long pressed Arab governments — most of which retain and use capital punishment — to follow the global abolition trend.
story.why: in a region where the death penalty is near-universal and often used for political and drug offences, a full legislative abolition sets a first regional precedent that campaigners will cite elsewhere, even as the change is legal rather than a shift in the underlying justice system.

story.headline: Car bomb kills Haftar intelligence chief
story.summary: A car bomb in Benghazi killed Fawzi al-Mansouri, military intelligence chief of Libya's eastern forces under Khalifa Haftar.
story.display_body: A car bomb killed Fawzi al-Mansouri, the military intelligence chief of Libya's eastern-based forces, in Benghazi on Tuesday 11 August — a rare high-level assassination inside the stronghold of commander Khalifa Haftar. The device detonated as al-Mansouri's car left evening prayers in the al-Hawari district; Haftar had appointed him to lead military intelligence in May 2024. No group claimed responsibility, and Khaled Haftar, the commander's son, said an investigation had opened and that "indicators point to a despicable terrorist tactic." The killing came the same day drones struck oil facilities in the divided country's east. Libya has been split since 2014 between the Haftar-led east and a UN-recognised government in Tripoli.
story.why: a strike this deep inside Haftar's security apparatus signals cracks in the east's tight internal control and complicates the stalled effort to reunify Libya's rival administrations.

story.headline: North Korea fires second missile in a week
story.summary: North Korea launched a ballistic missile, its second test in under a week, days before annual US–South Korea military drills.
story.display_body: North Korea fired a ballistic missile on Wednesday 12 August, its second launch in under a week, days before South Korea and the United States begin their annual joint military exercises. Seoul's military reported the launch; Pyongyang routinely times such tests to the allied drills, which it condemns as a rehearsal for invasion. The pair of launches breaks a relative lull and signals the North's objection to the coming exercises.
story.why: the tempo — two tests in a week, keyed to the drill calendar — is North Korea's familiar way of raising pressure without crossing into direct confrontation, and a marker of how little the diplomatic track has moved.

story.headline: Ukraine sends peace proposals to US
story.summary: Zelensky said Ukraine handed US negotiators proposals to end the war with Russia, and accused Moscow of readying an autumn mobilisation.
story.display_body: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Tuesday 11 August that Kyiv had handed US negotiators a set of proposals for ending the war with Russia, though he gave no details. In his nightly address he said Washington could help by strengthening Ukraine's air defences and by pressing Moscow "to prepare to end the war" rather than prolong it; both sides have signalled that US envoys may soon visit. Zelensky also accused Russia of readying a fresh large-scale mobilisation for the autumn, "immediately after the imitation of parliamentary elections" scheduled next month — a characterisation of Moscow's intent that Russia has not confirmed.
story.why: it is a concrete diplomatic move after a long stalemate, but with the proposals unpublished and no US visit yet scheduled, it remains a signal of intent rather than a breakthrough.

story.headline: Committee cuts EU wage-protection measure
story.summary: A Council of States committee voted 8-4 to strike the dismissal-protection measure from Switzerland's Bilaterals III wage-protection package, alarming the treaty's backers.
story.display_body: A Council of States committee voted on Tuesday 11 August to strike a worker-protection measure from Switzerland's domestic implementation of the Bilaterals III treaty package with the EU, prompting the package's backers to warn the compromise underpinning it is now at risk. By 8 votes to 4 with one abstention, the economic affairs committee of the Ständerat (WAK-S — the upper chamber's economic and tax committee) proposed dropping the fourteenth of the accompanying wage-protection measures: enhanced protection against dismissal for elected employee representatives. The committee argued the measure was "not directly connected" to the EU package and so did not belong among the wage-protection provisions; it also moved to soften rules on posting bonds and subcontractor liability for foreign firms. The Swiss Trade Union Federation (SGB) called the dismissal protection a "minimal solution" and an "indispensable part" of the deal. SP co-president Cédric Wermuth said he could "only read this as a frontal attack on Bilaterals III." The full Council of States takes up the wage-protection bill in the autumn session, with the National Council to follow.
story.why: the wage-protection measures were the social partners' negotiated price for accepting the EU package; unpicking them in committee reopens the domestic fight over free movement and could jeopardise ratification of a treaty set that governs how EU–CH relations affect work and residence in Switzerland.

story.headline: New tariff caps doctors' daily billing
story.summary: Specialists are protesting a per-workday billing ceiling in Switzerland's new TARDOC outpatient tariff, while GP groups say it barely affects them.
story.display_body: A cap on how much doctors can bill in a single working day, part of Switzerland's new outpatient tariff, is drawing loud protest from specialists, SRF reported on Wednesday 12 August. Under TARDOC — the ambulatory (non-hospital) medical fee schedule that replaced the decades-old TARMED tariff and took effect this year — the tariff partners (doctors', hospitals' and insurers' associations) agreed a ceiling of 1,577 tax points of physician work per working day, calculated on a maximum 12-hour day, as a cost-containment step ordered by Parliament. Specialists say the ceiling is set too low and will cut their incomes and penalise efficient practices, while GP and paediatric associations say it will barely touch primary care — exposing a split within the profession. The federal health office (BAG) has published an explainer on how the ceiling works.
story.why: the cap is one of the first concrete levers of the cost-containment drive meant to slow Switzerland's rising health premiums, and how it lands will shape both what specialists earn and how much of the ambulatory bill patients ultimately carry. (SRF, 12 Aug 2026; Federal Office of Public Health (BAG) )

story.headline: Bendahan enters Vaud government race
story.summary: Socialist national councillor Samuel Bendahan announced a bid in the PS primary for the 2027 Vaud Conseil d'Etat election.
story.display_body: Socialist heavyweight Samuel Bendahan announced on Wednesday 12 August that he will seek his party's nomination for the 2027 Vaud cantonal government, joining an already-crowded left-wing field. Bendahan, 46, a Lausanne economist who has sat in the National Council since 2017 and co-chairs the Social Democrats' (PS) parliamentary group, enters the party's primary under the slogan "For the freedom to live well." Fellow national councillor Jessica Jaccoud has also declared. Candidates have until 24 August to file, and the PS will settle its ticket at an extraordinary congress on 26 September in Aubonne.
story.why: the manoeuvring for the Conseil d'État — Vaud's seven-member executive — is opening early, and the PS primary will decide which of its federal-level figures the party sends into the 2027 cantonal race.

story.headline: Wandering black hole feeds on gravitational wake
story.summary: Evidence for a 35,000-solar-mass intermediate-mass black hole accreting gas from the dense wake its own gravity piles up as it wanders off-nucleus.
story.display_body: Supermassive black holes are thought to grow from "intermediate-mass" seeds of a few thousand to a few hundred thousand suns — and theory says many such seeds never make it to a galaxy's centre, instead wandering through their host after galaxy mergers fail to drag them inward. A nagging problem: a black hole parked in a galaxy's centre has gas funnelled onto it, but a wanderer drifting through thin interstellar gas shouldn't have much to eat. This team reports evidence for a wandering black hole of ~35,000 solar masses that is feeding anyway — by capturing gas from the dense wake its own gravity piles up behind it as it plows through the interstellar medium (the same gravitational-focusing effect that lets a moving mass gather a trailing overdensity). Multi-epoch spectroscopy resolves three gas components — a thin inflow ahead of the hole, a dense redshifted wake behind it, and thick absorbers close in that make its light flicker — matching the predicted geometry.
story.why: it is the first direct observational evidence for a fuel source that had only been predicted on paper, and it means these elusive middleweight black holes can grow while adrift — a channel that helps explain how the giants at galaxy centres got so big.

story.headline: DESI Legacy Survey maps four billion objects
story.summary: NOIRLab released the largest 2D sky map yet — three-quarters of the sky and nearly four billion catalogued objects, built over 13 years.
story.display_body: The DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys team released the newest and largest version of its map of the sky — 13 years in the making, covering three-quarters of the entire sky and cataloguing nearly four billion distinct objects: stars, galaxies, supernovae, gravitational lenses and more. The imaging comes from two U.S. National Science Foundation telescopes at Kitt Peak (Mayall) and Cerro Tololo in Chile (Blanco), the latter carrying the U.S. Department of Energy's Dark Energy Camera (DECam). The full catalogue is public, and it is the same imaging that selects targets for the DESI spectroscopic survey mapping cosmic expansion.
story.why: a free, sky-spanning catalogue of this depth is raw material for years of discovery — it is the finding chart the whole community, and increasingly automated surveys, mines for everything from rare lensed quasars to the next transient.

story.headline: JWST reads a young super-Jupiter's chemistry
story.summary: JWST spectroscopy of AF Lep b reveals sulfur enrichment implying the planet accreted ~56 Earth masses of solids during formation.
story.display_body: AF Lep b is one of the nearest young giant planets we can study directly — 3–4 Jupiter masses, orbiting ~9 AU (about Saturn's distance) from its star. Using JWST spectroscopy from 2.85–5.3 microns, the team detected carbon dioxide, hydrogen sulfide, methane, carbon monoxide (including its heavier ¹³CO isotope) and water in its atmosphere. Letting carbon, oxygen and sulfur abundances vary independently in the atmospheric fit — sulfur is a newer, powerful tracer because it is locked into dust and rock — they find the planet enriched ~3–5× above its star. That sulfur signature implies the planet swallowed roughly 56 Earth masses of solid material (ice and rock) as it formed, and its carbon-to-oxygen ratio points to formation near where it now sits rather than in the frigid outer disk.
story.why: sulfur is emerging as a "formation fingerprint," and here it lets astronomers reconstruct how a giant planet was built — a directly-imaged analog to the metal-enrichment story of Jupiter itself.

story.headline: Quadrupolar order drives hydride superconductor
story.summary: Calculations show a quadrupolar order parameter and soft phonons govern the structural transition tied to superconductivity in lanthanum hydride LaH10.
story.display_body: Lanthanum hydride (LaH₁₀) is the poster child of hydride superconductors — materials that carry current with zero resistance at a record-high 250 K (about −23 °C), but only when squeezed to ~170 GPa, roughly 1.7 million times atmospheric pressure. Everyone knew that as you compress it, its crystal changes shape (an R‑3m → Fm‑3m structural transition) right where superconductivity switches on, but why was unclear. This French–Japanese team ran the numbers — using a machine-learned interatomic potential (a neural network trained on quantum-mechanical energies, standing in for far slower first-principles simulation) — and found the transition is governed by a quadrupolar order parameter: the hydrogen atoms collectively adopt a subtle, four-lobed distortion pattern (think of the symmetry of a cloverleaf rather than a simple stretch). That "hidden order" softens a specific set of lattice vibrations (T₂g phonons) that happen to couple strongly to electrons — and strong electron–phonon coupling is exactly what glues electrons into the pairs that superconduct.
story.why: it hands materials designers a concrete knob — look for compounds with these soft quadrupolar distortions — in the hunt for a superconductor that works at everyday pressures, the field's holy grail.

story.headline: Faster estimate of quantum state entropy
story.summary: A new estimator measures the von Neumann entropy of an unknown quantum state with subquadratic samples, breaking a long-standing quadratic barrier.
story.display_body: The von Neumann entropy of a quantum state is its information-theoretic "temperature gauge" — it measures how mixed or uncertain the state is (zero for a pristine, fully-known state; large for a noisy or highly entangled one), and estimating it underlies benchmarking quantum computers and certifying entanglement. The catch: you can't read a quantum state off like a number; you have to prepare many identical copies and measure them, and every known method needed a number of copies growing as the square of the state's dimension d (written Ω(d²)) — a wall that plug-in estimators provably cannot beat. This paper gives the first estimator that breaks that quadratic barrier, needing o(d²) copies (asymptotically fewer than d²) for fixed accuracy, via a new "pinching" inequality plus tailored estimators for large and small eigenvalues.
story.why: copies of a quantum state are expensive to make, so shaving the sample cost of a routine diagnostic makes verifying real quantum hardware measurably cheaper — the first improvement on a bound that had stood as a hard limit.

story.headline: Bats socially learn winter hibernation sites
story.summary: 38 years of banding data on greater mouse-eared bats provide four lines of evidence that hibernaculum locations are socially transmitted.
story.display_body: Every autumn, temperate-zone bats fly long distances to gather at specific caves and mines to hibernate (the sites are called hibernacula). Biologists have long suspected each generation learns these locations from older bats rather than finding them by instinct — but hard evidence was missing. Researchers compiled 30,882 observations spanning 1985–2023 of 13,852 banded greater mouse-eared bats (Myotis myotis) and found four independent lines of evidence for social transmission: which hibernaculum an individual ends up using tracks the bats it associated with at summer roosts, not simply the nearest site or its birthplace. It is one of the longest-baseline datasets ever brought to bear on the question of animal "culture."
story.why: if bats inherit migration knowledge socially rather than genetically, losing the older, knowledgeable individuals in a colony — to disease like white-nose syndrome or to disturbance of a single cave — can erase a route the population can't quickly relearn, a real consideration for European conservation.

story.headline: How some escape a genetic Alzheimer's fate
story.summary: A deep single-nucleus study of the entorhinal cortex finds oligogenic resilience to PSEN1 E280A autosomal-dominant Alzheimer's in protected carriers.
story.display_body: In an extended Colombian family, thousands of people carry a single mutation (PSEN1 E280A) that all but guarantees early-onset Alzheimer's in their 40s — making them a natural experiment for the disease. A few members are mysteriously spared for decades, and the standout case, a man carrying a rare variant nicknamed RELN‑COLBOS, stayed dementia-free ~20 years past the expected onset. This team dissected the entorhinal cortex — the memory-circuit region where Alzheimer's pathology typically begins — in protected and unprotected carriers using single-nucleus and spatial transcriptomics (techniques that read which genes are switched on, cell by cell and in place within the tissue) plus whole-genome sequencing. They report that resilience looks oligogenic — the combined effect of several rare variants rather than one — and find unusual cell populations in the protected brain: RELN‑positive inhibitory interneurons enriched in the cortex's top layer and abundant ADAMTSL1‑positive excitatory neurons, hinting at a preserved, rewired local circuit.
story.why: people who resist a disease they are genetically fated to get are the best possible pointer to a treatment; mapping the cells and genes behind their protection is how you turn a lucky biology into a drug target. As a single-family preprint, it is a mechanistic lead, not proof.
